text: Caradoc's real-world test set is 10000 PDFs found through search-engine queries built from random English dictionary words.
quote: extracted randomly from an English dictionary. In total, we gathered 10000 files.

text: Only 1465 of the real-world files were accepted by Caradoc's strict syntactic rules.
quote: We first tested the validation chain directly. Only 1465 files were accepted by our strict syntactic

text: Most real-world files used incremental updates, which the strict subset forbids, and some had several successive updates.
quote: the majority of the files made use of incremental updates, that were not allowed by our restrictions. Some files even contained several successive updates

text: Caradoc's normalizer removes every object not reachable from the trailer and renumbers objects contiguously from zero; it rewrote 8993 of 10000 files.
quote: Our normalization tool then removed all objects that were not accessible from the trailer and renumbered the objects in a continuous range starting from zero. In total, we could rewrite 8993 files out of 10000.

text: Real-world files had ill-formed xref tables that declared in-use objects at offset zero instead of using free-entry syntax.
quote: The invalid files that we found incorrectly declared in-use objects at offset zero instead of using the appropriate syntax for free objects.

text: The offset-zero xref bug was common enough that the authors added an ad hoc tolerance option to normalize such files.
quote: since this bug was common, we decided to add an ad hoc option to accept this mistake and be able to normalize the files in question.

text: Semantic equivalence of normalized files to their originals was checked only manually, on a restricted set of files, by opening them in readers and comparing the graphical result.
quote: we checked manually – i.e. on a restricted set of files – that the normalized files could effectively be opened in PDF readers and that the graphical result was the same

text: Tolerance options covered only common bugs, not every possible mistake, so some real-world files could not be normalized.
quote: We implemented similar options for common bugs that we noticed, but did not intent to correct every possible mistake. Thus, some files could not be normalized.

text: An ill-formed name escape (/Foo#7/Bar) is read as one name by some readers and as two by others, which let the authors build a file with totally different interpretations among readers.
quote: some readers see one name token whereas others see two names: /Foo#7 and /Bar. This allowed us to create a file with totally different interpretations among readers.

text: When no object matches a reference's object and generation numbers, some readers ignore the generation number and resolve by object number alone.
quote: When no object corresponds to the pair of numbers, some readers discard the generation number and look for an object with the same object number.

text: Given a dictionary with a duplicated key, none of the tested readers reported an error and all used the second value.
quote: none of the tested software reported an error, but instead, all of them associated the key /Key with the second value

text: Mainstream readers accept flawed files and silently try to correct the errors themselves.
quote: One of the biggest issues of current PDF readers is that they accept flawed files and try to correct the errors by themselves.

text: Caradoc does not validate most stream filters (only Flate is decoded), leaving stream-encoding checks out of scope.
quote: Currently, we do not check most of them because the inherent complexity of compression formats goes beyond the scope of our work.

text: The authors built an ill-formed file that crashed some readers yet was reported well-formed and valid by JHOVE's PDF module.
quote: we were able to create an ill-formed file that caused a crash on some readers but was nevertheless reported as “well-formed and valid” by

text: The authors found no open-source PDF parser built with lexer and parser generators; all were ad hoc.
quote: In our study, we did not find any open source PDF parser relying on lexer and parser generators.

text: Cyclic object structures can trigger infinite recursion in most readers.
quote: In particular, cyclic structures can trigger infinite recursion on most readers.

text: Outlines containing cycles made most tested readers loop indefinitely on at least one file.
quote: Most of them looped indefinitely for at least one file.

text: The specification does not require an incremental update to be located after its predecessor, so /Prev chains can form loops (issue found by Bogk et al.).
quote: In particular, an update is not required to be located before its predecessor in the file.

text: 16 of the 29 tested PDF viewers, including Adobe Acrobat and Foxit Reader, were vulnerable to shadow attacks.
quote: Our results reveal that 16 (including Adobe Acrobat and Foxit Reader) of the 29 PDF viewers tested were vulnerable to shadow attacks.

text: Shadow attacks abuse only legitimate PDF features rather than viewer implementation bugs, which makes them hard to mitigate.
quote: Since shadow attacks abuse only legitimate features, they are hard to mitigate.

text: The first Hide-and-Replace variant places two objects with the same object number but different content in the file, with the signed xref pointing at the harmless one.
quote: create a PDF file containing two objects with the same object ID (e.g., 4 0 obj) but different content

text: After signing, an appended xref that re-points an object number to content already inside the signed area raises no warning and the signature still validates.
quote: Since the inclusion of an Xref table pointing to an already defined object within the signed area is considered harmless, there is no warning of the changes made.

text: The second Hide-and-Replace variant toggles objects between in-use and free in an appended xref, changing what is shown without altering any object.
quote: By this means, attackers can hide “in use” objects and show “free” objects. This is possible without changing the objects themselves.

text: PDF-Detector detects Hide, Hide-and-Replace and overlay Replace attacks by comparing the document with its state at the first signature, i.e. with all later incremental updates removed.
quote: This comparison can be technically implemented by removing all data, that is, all Incremental Updates, after the first signature.

text: PDF-Detector was verified and tuned only on 26 PDF documents (the authors' own generated exploits and controls).
quote: We were able to verify and fine-tune the correct analysis based on these 26 PDF documents

text: The authors plan to train PDF-Detector on additional documents to raise detection and lower false positives.
quote: We plan to train the tool with additional documents to strengthen the detection rate and minimize the false positive rate.

text: Replace-class shadow content cannot be flagged before signing, because injecting it is indistinguishable from benign content.
quote: For the Replace category, a prevention phase cannot be sensibly implemented. The first step “injecting shadow content” is indistinguishable from a benign injection.

text: Text selection, copy-paste or search may expose shadow content that the rendered page hides.
quote: further actions like text selection, copy-pasting text, or searching within the document might expose the attack’s stealthiness.

text: The earlier Incremental Saving Attacks appended malformed incremental updates with missing or unclosed objects.
quote: ISAs manipulate a PDF by appending a malformed Incremental Update, wherein objects are missing or not closed properly.

text: 13.5% of real-world Govdocs1 PDF files are rendered inconsistently by at least one popular reader.
quote: such inconsistencies are common—13.5% PDF files are inconsistently rendered by at least one popular reader.

text: The manual study used a one-percent random sample of 2,313 Govdocs1 documents, each opened in eight graphical readers.
quote: Thus, we study a one percent random sample of 2,313 documents. We open each document with the eight graphical PDF readers

text: Without known originals, correctness was decided by majority: if five or more readers agree, they are taken as correct and the others incorrect.
quote: If five readers or more have identical renderings and the others display the page differently, we consider the five readers to be correct and the others incorrect.

text: Only first pages were compared, so the true share of inconsistent files is likely larger than 13.5%.
quote: Since only the first pages of those documents have been studied, and an inconsistency can happen anywhere in the document, the number of inconsistencies would likely be bigger than 13.5% when all pages of the documents are considered.

text: Identical error messages do not imply identical output: readers with different recovery strategies can emit the same errors yet render differently, so visual comparison is needed.
quote: two readers may emit identical error messages for one file, but this file may still be displayed differently by the two readers because they have different recovery strategies to address the error.

text: A bug that makes all readers fail identically (e.g. the same wrong image) is invisible to cross-reader comparison.
quote: If one PDF file exposes the same bug in all readers, and causes all readers to fail in the same way (e.g., all display an identical but wrong image), our approach would fail to detect this bug as there are no visual inconsistencies.

text: The authors plan to automatically fix the PDF files whose bugs cause cross-reader inconsistencies.
quote: In the future, we plan to automatically fix the detected bugs in PDF files to ensure consistency across readers.

text: They note that fixing PDF files is hard because the xref table lists object offsets and objects cross-reference each other by number.
quote: Fixing PDF documents is not a trivial task due to document format constraints such as cross-reference table that lists object offsets in the file

text: Reader developers often add workaround patches so that readers tolerate malformed files.
quote: we learned that in many cases, developers are willing to provide workaround patches to the readers to tolerate bugs in malformed

text: The automated inconsistency detector reached 33% precision, 60% recall and 43% F1.
quote: The detection precision, recall and F1 for our approach are 33%, 60%, and 43% respectively.

text: None of the sampled Govdocs1 PDFs conformed to PDF/A or PDF/X.
quote: we found that none of these files conformed to the PDF/A or PDF/X standards

text: Flattening a PDF to avoid display differences can itself add inconsistencies when layers are merged.
quote: flattening a PDF file may add more inconsistencies when merging the different layers of the original file

text: The SafeDocs test-and-evaluation corpus has an internet_sourced subset drawn from Common Crawl and a separate hand-curated dangerous set.
quote: The internet_sourced set is a subset of Common Crawl [11], while the dangerous set is a

text: Table I: the internet_sourced set has 9000 files, of which experts marked 7206 valid and 1794 rejected (non-compliant or malicious).
1794 files in the Common Crawl-derived internet_sourced set were 'misclassified', i.e. expert-marked rejected.
quote: There are 1794 misclassified files in the internet_sourced set and 488 misclassified files in the dangerous set.

text: Without normative repair rules, parsers repair non-compliant files differently and a malicious file can exploit those differences, so SafeDocs T&E rejected all benign-but-non-compliant files.
quote: Absent this guidance, different parsers may perform different repairs, resulting in different behaviors. Because a malicious file can be crafted to exploit these differences, it was deemed safer to mark all such files as “rejected”.

text: Many parsers attempt to repair non-compliant files so they can be rendered.
quote: Indeed, many parsers will attempt to repair non-compliant files so that they can be rendered.

text: Flagging non-compliant or malicious files against benign ones had a false reporting rate of roughly 5%.
quote: In the former case, we found a false reporting rate of roughly 5%.

text: Aside from a few similar parsers, PDF parsers' error behaviours are not redundant, so using all available parsers is most informative.
quote: there is not much redundancy present in the behaviors of parsers for the PDF specification

text: The datasets contain compliant files, files with benign correctable malformations, files that could not be corrected, and intentionally malicious files.
quote: The datasets discussed in this paper contained fully compliant files, files with “benign” malformations that could be correctd, files that could not be corrected, and some files that were intentionally malicious.

text: Unsupervised bootstrapping of compliant/non-compliant samples from one aggregated sample needs further investigation.
quote: it might be possible to use an unsupervised bootstrapping approach to extract the two samples of files from a single aggregated sample. This requires further investigation.

text: The PDF specification is acknowledged to be ambiguous in places and has many proprietary extensions.
quote: It is recognized that the specification is ambiguous in places, and that there are many proprietary extensions to the specification.

text: Common Crawl truncates files at 1 MB; in the December 2019 crawl nearly 430,000 PDFs (22%) were truncated.
quote: Common Crawl truncates files at 1 MB. If researchers require intact files, they must re-pull truncated files from the original websites. In the December, 2019 crawl, nearly 430,000 PDFs (22%) were truncated.

text: SafeDocs harvested parser-stressing files from issue trackers, e.g. querying Ghostscript's Bugzilla API for issues with application-type attachments.
quote: the team used Bugzilla’s API to query for issues that contained attachments with mime-types including the term

text: In CC-MAIN-2021-31, Common Crawl flagged 2,020,913 PDF URLs as truncated because of length.
quote: `length` (2,020,913) -- the file was truncated because of length

text: A further 5,861 PDF captures were truncated by a network disconnection during Common Crawl's fetch.
quote: `disconnect` (5,861) -- there was a network disconnection during Common Crawl's original fetch

text: SafeDocs successfully refetched 1,922,505 URLs from the original target URL.
quote: `REFETCHED_SUCCESS` (1,922,505) -- our project refetched content from the original target URL

text: The provenance table records the Common Crawl WARC file and offsets of each URL's original capture, so the truncated capture can be retrieved alongside the refetched file.
quote: `cc_warc_start` -- the offset within the `cc_warc_file` where the individual warc file is stored

text: Common Crawl truncates files at 1 MB; the corpus replaces them with complete files refetched from the original URLs without a size limit.
quote: Common Crawl truncates files at 1MB. For this corpus, we refetched the complete/untruncated PDF files from the original URLs without any file size limitation.

text: Common Crawl recorded 6,383,873 of the PDF URLs as not truncated.
quote: `''` (6,383,873) -- (empty string) -- Common Crawls records this as not truncated

text: The provenance table has 8,410,704 rows including the header, one per URL.
quote: The table `cc-provenance-20230303.csv.gz` contains all provenance information from the crawl (8,410,704 rows, including the header).

text: Representativeness of the corpus for PDFs on the web or in general cannot be rigorously assessed.
quote: It is not possible to rigorously assess how representative this corpus is of all PDF files on the entire web or of PDF files in general.

text: Selection by HTTP Content-Type or detected MIME admits some files that are not actually PDFs.
quote: We acknowledge that this choice will result in files that are not actually PDFs.

text: Charter 3(a) uses cross-engine agreement as a robustness metric for found files, but engines share recovery heuristics (duplicate keys resolved identically, CLM-0210; generation-number fallback, CLM-0209) and common-mode failures are invisible to agreement (CLM-0245); agreement is not correctness, and 13.5% of intact real files already disagree (CLM-0240).

CDR-style normalization (drop unreachable objects, renumber: CLM-0203) is omission by design under charter §2 and destroys exactly the revision evidence that shadow-attack detection needs (CLM-0225); PDFPundit's emitter must not inherit this default.

Refetched files plus their original truncated Common Crawl captures (CLM-0282, CLM-0283) form candidate natural pairs, but a later refetch may return a changed document; a pair is usable only if the capture is a byte prefix of the refetched file.
